$comment: Shared built-in CORS conformance table.
The `middleware.builtin.cors` block is applied by two hosts that cannot share
code, and a project is served by whichever one it was deployed to:
- crates/ruvyxa_middleware/src/{config,builtin}.rs   (`dev`, `start`, `preview`)
- packages/ruvyxa/runtime/serverless-handler.mjs     (every serverless adapter)
They had disagreed. The Rust config filled `methods` with an implicit
GET/POST/PUT/DELETE/OPTIONS when a project named none, and the JavaScript
handler had no such default — so `cors: { origins: [...] }` with no `methods`
answered a cross-origin PUT preflight with the method list under `ruvyxa dev`
and with no `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` at all once deployed, which the
browser reads as a blocked request. Nothing failed a build or appeared in a
log; the split only showed up in a browser pointed at production.
The narrower behavior is the shared one. `docs/en/13-security.md` already asks
a project to name its origins, methods, and headers explicitly, and closing
the gap the other way would have widened the cross-origin surface of every
deployed application that had relied on the default without asking for it.
Every implementation replays this file:
- crates/ruvyxa_middleware/src/config.rs                (Rust test)
- tests/packages/ruvyxa/cors-contract.test.mjs          (JavaScript test)
Add a case here first when changing what the built-in CORS layer sends; a port
that drifts then fails in the language that drifted rather than in a browser.
$defaultsNote: What each field means when the project's config omits it. `methods` and
`headers` are empty rather than populated: an empty list sends no header, so
neither host advertises an allowance the project never wrote down.
$placementNote: and the Fetch standard has the browser read them only from a preflight
response. Sending them on an actual response advertises the whole allowlist to
any origin that gets a response at all, and invites a shared cache to store a
`Max-Age` that was never negotiated. `Allow-Origin` and `Allow-Credentials` do
belong on both, because the browser checks those on the actual response too.
$varyNote: The response body is identical but its CORS headers depend on the request
Origin, so `Vary: Origin` belongs on the rejected path as well. Without it a
shared cache can store the header-less response and replay it to an allowed
origin, which reads to the browser as a random CORS failure.
$credentialedWildcardNote: `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` alongside a reflected wildcard origin
lets any site read authenticated responses. Both hosts refuse, at the earliest
point each one can: the native server rejects the configuration before it
binds a port, and the handler — which is handed a config it cannot reject,
because a deployed function has no startup to fail in — treats no origin as
allowed and sends no CORS headers at all. Different mechanism, same outcome:
no origin is ever granted credentialed access through a wildcard.
